name: Kubernetes / Container Hunt
author: Platform Security Team
prerequisites: kubectl access with at least cluster-reader ClusterRole
Kubernetes audit logging enabled and forwarded to SIEM
Access to container runtime logs (Docker daemon or containerd)
required_tools: Splunk or Elastic with K8s audit log index

hunt_actions.title: Unauthorized Container and Workload Activity
actions: List all running containers and identify unrecognized images: `kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq -r '.items[] | {namespace: .metadata.namespace, pod: .metadata.name, image: .spec.containers[].image}' | jq -s 'unique_by(.image) | .[] | select(.image | test("approved-registry") | not)'` — replace approved-registry with your registry FQDN; flag any pod using images from DockerHub or unknown registries.

Detect privileged containers and host namespace sharing: `kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq -r '.items[] | select(.spec.containers[].securityContext.privileged==true or .spec.hostPID==true or .spec.hostNetwork==true or .spec.hostIPC==true) | {namespace: .metadata.namespace, pod: .metadata.name}'` — any privileged pod not in the approved list (e.g., node exporters, DaemonSets) requires immediate investigation.

Hunt for containers with mounted host paths: `kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq -r '.items[] | select(.spec.volumes[]?.hostPath != null) | {ns: .metadata.namespace, pod: .metadata.name, path: [.spec.volumes[].hostPath.path // empty]}'` — host mounts of /etc, /var/run/docker.sock, or / indicate a breakout attempt or misconfiguration.

Check for recently created or modified CronJobs and Jobs: `kubectl get cronjobs -A -o wide; kubectl get jobs -A --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp | tail -20` — review schedules and image sources for any unauthorized workloads; also: `kubectl describe cronjob <name> -n <ns>` to inspect the full job spec.

hunt_actions.title: RBAC and Secrets Access Abuse
actions: Audit RBAC bindings for overly permissive roles: `kubectl get clusterrolebindings -o json | jq -r '.items[] | select(.roleRef.name=="cluster-admin") | {binding: .metadata.name, subjects: .subjects}'` — cluster-admin should be bound only to the absolute minimum set of service accounts and human accounts; compare against approved list.

Detect secret enumeration activity in K8s audit logs: Splunk: `index=k8s_audit verb=list OR verb=get objectRef.resource=secrets user.username!=system:kube-controller-manager user.username!=system:kube-scheduler | stats count by user.username, objectRef.namespace | sort -count` — any non-system account listing or reading secrets in bulk is high priority.

Hunt for service account token mounts in unauthorized pods: `kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq -r '.items[] | select(.spec.automountServiceAccountToken==true or .spec.automountServiceAccountToken==null) | {ns: .metadata.namespace, pod: .metadata.name, sa: .spec.serviceAccountName}'` — then check each service account's RBAC rights with `kubectl describe clusterrolebinding | grep -A5 <serviceaccount>`.

Identify new ClusterRole or Role bindings created in last 30 days: `kubectl get clusterrolebindings --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp -o json | jq -r '.items[-10:] | .[] | {name: .metadata.name, created: .metadata.creationTimestamp, role: .roleRef.name, subjects: .subjects}'` — cross-reference against approved RBAC change log.

hunt_actions.title: Container Escape and Node Compromise
actions: Check for suspicious processes running inside containers via Falco: Review Falco alert output for rules: 'Terminal shell in container', 'Contact K8S API Server From Container', 'Netcat Remote Code Execution', or 'Write below root'. Falco log location: `journalctl -u falco -f` or `kubectl logs -n falco -l app=falco --since=24h`

Detect container escape via docker.sock mount: `find / -name 'docker.sock' -type s 2>/dev/null` — if docker.sock is mounted inside a container and accessible to the container process, full host compromise is trivial. Verify: `ls -la /var/run/docker.sock` and `docker inspect <container_id> | jq '.[].Mounts[] | select(.Source=="/var/run/docker.sock")'`

Hunt for cryptomining indicators in container CPU usage: `kubectl top pods -A | sort -k3 -rn | head -20` — pods with sustained CPU > 80% when not under load, or `docker stats --no-stream | sort -k3 -rn | head -10` — cross-reference high-CPU containers with their image and network connections using `docker exec <container_id> ss -tnp`

questions: Is Kubernetes API server audit logging enabled and configured to capture at least RequestResponse level for the secrets, configmaps, pods, and exec API groups, and are logs forwarded to the SIEM?
Is Falco or an equivalent Kubernetes runtime threat detection tool deployed as a DaemonSet on all nodes, and are alerts forwarded to the security operations team in real time?
Is a container image scanning tool (Trivy, Prisma Cloud, Sysdig) integrated into the CI/CD pipeline to block deployment of images with Critical-severity vulnerabilities?
Are Pod Security Admission (PSA) policies or a third-party admission controller (OPA Gatekeeper, Kyverno) enforcing restrictions on privileged containers, hostPath mounts, and host namespace sharing?

Is the Kubernetes RBAC model formally documented, and is the principle of least privilege enforced such that no service accounts or user accounts have cluster-admin unless explicitly justified and approved?

Are Kubernetes secrets stored in etcd encrypted at rest (kube-apiserver --encryption-provider-config), and are secrets also managed through an external secrets manager (HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager)?
Is network policy enforced within the cluster to restrict pod-to-pod communication to only approved paths (deny-all default NetworkPolicy with explicit allow rules per namespace)?
Are container images sourced exclusively from an internal, approved registry with image signing (Cosign/Notary) enforced via admission control, preventing unsigned or external images from running?
